one_line: Exa's CEO pitches Exa as a search engine built for AI agents rather than humans, covering its history, API features (fast endpoint, token extraction, structured output) and a data marketplace.
summary: Will Bryk, co-founder of Exa (formerly Metaphor), argues that AI agents will soon make more web searches than humans and that they need a different kind of search than Google, which was built for humans. He tells the company story: started in 2021 betting that transformer embeddings could make semantic search work, launched a search product in 2022, and found that developers wanted an API for LLMs. He describes current product features: a roughly 200 ms search endpoint for voice agents, token extraction that returns only the most relevant tokens from search results to cut LLM cost, structured-output search for list-building, and per-customer configuration of domains, time windows and speed versus quality. He also presents Exa Connect, a marketplace where data providers license private data to agent developers. The talk is mostly vision and company promotion, with few technical details or evidence for its headline numbers.

key_ideas.idea: AI systems will soon issue more searches than humans, and the gap is expected to grow to about 1000x.
key_ideas.detail: The speaker's framing: AI searches overtake human searches in 2026, then grow far faster. This is a forecast with no source shown in the talk.

key_ideas.idea: Google-style search is built for humans and behaves like a recommender, so it fails on set-complete queries.
key_ideas.detail: Examples: 'shirts without stripes' returns striped shirts, and 'everyone in Singapore who works on AI search' returns documents, not a full list of matches. Agents need database-like completeness.

key_ideas.idea: Running an LLM over every document for every query is too expensive, so the work is to pre-index documents with embeddings.
key_ideas.detail: The thought experiment: an LLM judging a trillion documents per search would cost about $10M per query. Embeddings let you precompute document representations and then query them cheaply, usually combined with keyword matching.

key_ideas.idea: The business model came from LLM developers asking for a search API, because models cannot hold the whole web and must retrieve.
key_ideas.detail: Speaker's claim: even very large models are tiny relative to the web, so they always need a retrieval layer. AI systems want near-database access, not SEO or ads.

key_ideas.idea: Agent-facing search needs tunable latency: a very fast endpoint for voice, and slower, deeper queries that can run for minutes.
key_ideas.detail: The speaker says a voice agent can't afford search latency, so Exa offers an endpoint around 200 ms. Other customers accept minutes of search time in exchange for higher quality.

key_ideas.idea: Token extraction returns the most relevant passages from search results, not full snippets, to reduce downstream LLM spend.
key_ideas.detail: Example: from 10 documents, return about 100 of the most important tokens. The speaker frames this as a way to address the compute and token-cost problem.

key_ideas.idea: Structured output lets the search return typed fields extracted from pages, such as a paper's citation count or a person's education.
key_ideas.detail: Example: a recruiting agent asks for engineers who recently left a big lab, with their most-cited paper, college and graduation year, returned as structured data.

key_ideas.idea: There is no single perfect search. Each customer effectively gets its own configured search, with knobs for domain allow and deny lists, time windows, product-page exclusion and speed versus quality.
key_ideas.detail: The speaker says Exa runs roughly one search configuration per customer, with the customer choosing the tradeoffs.

key_ideas.idea: Exa Connect adds licensed private or paid data providers to search results, creating a market where data owners set prices and developers pick sources.
key_ideas.detail: Example shown: combining public web results with Similarweb traffic data that is not publicly available. The speaker describes this as a free market for agent-accessible data.

techniques.name: Hybrid embedding plus keyword retrieval
techniques.how: Precompute embeddings for each document so a query can be matched semantically without running a model per document, and combine with keyword matching where embeddings alone fall short.
techniques.when: Retrieval over a large corpus where queries are complex or semantic and per-document model calls are too costly.

techniques.name: Token-budget extraction before the LLM
techniques.how: Take the top-k retrieved documents and return only the top N tokens (e.g. about 100 from 10 docs) instead of full pages or long snippets.
techniques.when: An agent needs grounding but the LLM context and cost must stay small.

techniques.name: Schema-based structured search output
techniques.how: Ask the search to return named fields (e.g. paper citations, education, graduation year) for each matching entity, not free-text passages.
techniques.when: Agents that build lists or databases of people, companies or papers.

techniques.name: Per-tenant search configuration
techniques.how: Expose knobs per customer: include or exclude domains, date windows, product-page filtering, and a speed versus quality setting.
techniques.when: A multi-tenant search service where each customer's agent has different accuracy, latency and source needs.

techniques.name: Latency tiers by consumer type
techniques.how: Offer a very fast search path for real-time voice agents and a slow, high-quality path for background research that may take minutes.
techniques.when: One retrieval service serving both interactive and batch agent workloads.

numbers.claim: Web searches by AI systems expected to exceed human searches in 2026, then grow about 1000x over the next few years (speaker forecast, no source given).
Over 5,000 companies and over 400,000 developers use Exa.
The web is on the order of a trillion pages.
Running a neural model over a trillion documents per query would cost about $10M per search (speaker's estimate).
Company raised a couple million dollars and spent about half on a GPU cluster early on.
Search endpoint latency of about 200 ms.
Token extraction example: from 10 retrieved documents, return about 100 tokens.
Progress in a quarter or two now equals the previous five years of progress (speaker's claim).

hot_takes: AI systems will soon search far more than humans, roughly 1000x, and search should be built for them rather than for people.
Search for AI should not be ad-driven or SEO-driven; AI systems want an almost database-like view of the world's information.
Keyword search and recommendation-style ranking can't answer complete, set-based queries, so embedding-based search is needed.
Information access is the key unsolved problem, and better search is needed to prevent manipulation and poor collective decisions.

relevance.why: MemoryMesh (L2A) does hybrid BM25 plus pgvector retrieval. The talk's token-budget extraction is one retrieval-side pattern to compare against it, but the talk gives no measurements.
relevance.action: In the MemoryMesh retrieval path, add an optional top-N token trim on retrieved chunks, then compare LLM token cost and answer quality with and without it on the existing RAGAS eval set.

relevance.why: No content on checkpointing, plan/critique loops, skill ranking, or credential handling.
